If you were God, how would the world be different? If I were the Almighty, the world would be an entirely different place, a veritable paradise compared to the dystopian nightmare we currently inhabit. First and foremost, there would be no war, no violence, no hatred. Every man, woman, and child would live in peace and harmony with one another, respecting each other's differences and celebrating their shared humanity. Hunger and poverty would be eradicated. No one would go without the basic necessities of life - food, shelter, and clothing - as resources would be distributed fairly and equitably. Disease would be a thing of the past. I would eliminate all illnesses, ensuring that everyone enjoyed perfect health and vitality. The environment would be pristine, with clean air and water, lush forests, and vibrant ecosystems. The Earth would be a true Garden of Eden, a testament to the beauty and wonder of creation. Furthermore, there would be no liars nor hypocrites. Every government leader would be honest in an ethical manner. Humanity would walk the tight rope of righteousness. The love of Jesus Christ would be in their hearts and on their lips.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? The Bible says that Enoch and Elijah, neither of whom died, went to Heaven. But did the Bible tell us about any other human beings who avoided death and went directly to the kingdom of the Lord? The scriptures indicate that Moses, too, went to Heaven, although in a less spectacular way. Deuteronomy 34 gives us the story behind this amazing event. "Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the Lord showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan, all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the Western Sea, the Negev, and the plain, the Valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar. Then the Lord said to him, "This is the land which I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'I will give it to your descendants.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there." So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord. And He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows his grave to this day." (Deuteronomy 34:1-6) If you read these six verses carefully you will realize that they do not actually tell us that Moses died. The Lord says he will not let Moses enter the Promised Land, but doesn't say he won't be entering Heaven. The text tells us that Moses died "according to the word of the Lord," and was buried. And that is all the Holy Bible actually says about the death of Moses. The story of Moses' death ends, not with his demise, but with a mystery. The mystery of what happened next. The New Testament may well hold the answer. In the Gospel of Luke 9, we are told that Moses and Elijah appeared to Jesus on the Mount of Transfiguration. The Bible tells us that Elijah escaped death by being taken directly to Heaven. We know that Enoch avoided death and went directly to Heaven. And now we know that Moses also avoided being kept in the grave. The other alternative is that Moses' soul went to Heaven. But both Moses and Elijah had bodies, because the Bible tells us that Jesus spoke to them.

If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? If Jesus was fully God and therefore fully human, did he have a mother? Yes! But how can one be God and not have a father? How is Jesus the Son of God? That is the mystery of God. We know this is not a mystery, but a lie when it comes to the supposed "Second Coming" of God. What is the biggest secret in the history of Trump? Trump's father, Fred Trump, was a KKK member and arrested for causing an attack on police officers at a Klan rally, but the New York newspapers reported the arrest took place at the Trump residence, according to reports. According to the New York Times, the Trump organization was sued in 1973 by the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division for refusing to rent apartments to black people, and Trump reportedly said to the Justice Department’s lawyers, "I will never settle this case." And yet, many evangelicals will vote for Trump. Why don’t they see the evil? Was Trump elected president because of the Christian right's hatred of Hillary Clinton and Hillary Clinton's association with Bill Clinton's infidelity? Evangelical Christians should vote for a person who will do as Jesus Christ would do, and that is not Donald Trump. Was the Jan. 6 rebellion a coup attempt? Or, in light of the fact that Trump knew the election was rigged and was stolen, was Jan. 6 a protest and a warning? If Trump knew the election was rigged, why didn't Trump ever release all the evidence he said he had? Why did Trump repeatedly tell the American people lies about the election? Why should anyone trust Trump? Is it safe to assume Trump is going to be the next president of the United States? I doubt it! The Bible says the antichrist will make himself out to be something he isn’t.

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? Let's begin by examining what the historical sources tell us. It is widely accepted that the Roman historian Tacitus and the Jewish historian Josephus wrote about a man named Jesus of Nazareth. However, there are many things that we cannot know with certainty. For instance, while the Gospels describe Jesus as a miracle worker, no contemporaneous external source confirms those accounts, and skeptics dismiss them as embellishments or falsehoods. The Gospels are the best source for reconstructing the life of Jesus, but they were written decades after his supposed death, so the authors may have been working purely on oral tradition. The Gospels don't present one consistent picture either, with Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John offering somewhat contradictory accounts. Also, the earliest writings of the Apostle Paul, the first Christian author, are silent regarding the details of Jesus’s earthly life. Instead, Paul focuses exclusively on Jesus’s death and resurrection. A major problem for those who attempt to use historical methods to determine the truth or falsehood of the Bible is that it is difficult to prove or disprove miracles, a fundamental aspect of Christian belief. If you accept the miracles, you've accepted the Bible. If you don't, you still have an uphill climb.

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? That is simple enough. He used his divine power, his holy abilities, to transform the ordinary into the extraordinary. The miracle at Cana is one of the many examples of Jesus demonstrating His deity. No one else could do such a thing. How could a mere mortal turn water into wine? Only God could have performed that miracle, as the true-born Son of God. This first public act of Christ, according to the Gospel of John, was a demonstration of His glory, of His divinity, of His inherent power, and it was also a display of compassion; Jesus was not merely showing off. He cared that the wedding feast would continue without disruption. He wanted people to experience joy and merriment, not disappointment or embarrassment. Jesus' first miracle was a testament to His ability to change things, to transform a situation, and to provide for those in need. Even though the wedding hosts had run out of wine, Jesus intervened, and the party went on. Imagine the look on the faces of the wedding guests when they tasted the new wine! Was it better than the first? The headwaiter was certainly impressed. He told the groom: "Everyone brings out the choice wine first and then the cheaper wine after the guests have had too much to drink; but you have saved the best till now." (John 2:10). What a testament to Jesus’ miraculous capabilities!

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? In a nation steeped in a rich literary heritage, a vibrant constellation of contemporary Russian poets continues to illuminate the poetic landscape. Among the most compelling is Vera Pavlova, whose elegant and erudite verses often explore themes of love, loss, and the transcendent. Her poems are frequently characterized by their delicate imagery, precise language, and deep emotional resonance. Then there is Dmitry Prigov, a controversial yet hugely influential figure whose work, steeped in postmodern irony and linguistic experimentation, deconstructs Soviet-era ideologies and explores the absurdities of modern life. His verses, often imbued with wit and political commentary, challenge traditional poetic forms. Further, Marina Temkina, known for her evocative portrayals of urban life and her sensitive observations of human relationships, writes poems that resonate with a unique blend of realism and lyricism. Her work often explores the nuances of everyday experiences with a keen eye for detail. Not to be overlooked is Lev Rubinstein. His conceptual poetry, characterized by its use of index cards and performance elements, subverts traditional notions of poetic practice, while offering insightful reflections on history, memory, and the nature of language itself. Each of these poets, in their distinct voices and styles, contributes to the vitality and diversity of the contemporary Russian poetic scene.

What is a poem on the moon in any specific language? Absolutely! The moon has held a certain mystique for poets across civilizations, inspiring countless verses. Here's a poem in Spanish, with a loose English translation:**Spanish:***Luna llena, faro en la noche,**testigo eterno del amor y el dolor,**tu luz plateada, un suave broche,**que adorna el firmamento con su fulgor.**Sobre campos y mares te derramas,**un manto etéreo, suave y sutil,**mientras los amantes se enamoran,**y el lobo aúlla en su juvenil* *túnel.**En tu danza cósmica, silenciosa,**guardas secretos de un tiempo atrás,**la historia del mundo, majestuosa,**escrita en sombras y en claridad.***English Translation:***Full moon, beacon in the night,**eternal witness of love and pain,**your silver light, a gentle brooch,**that adorns the firmament with its glow.**Over fields and seas you pour,**an ethereal mantle, soft and subtle,**while lovers fall in love,**and the wolf howls in its youthful tunnel.**In your cosmic dance, silent,**you keep secrets of a time past,**the history of the world, majestic,**written in shadows and clarity.*

How could Adam and Eve be white when the first humans lived in Africa? The skin color of Adam and Eve is irrelevant. The Bible does not specify the skin color of the first humans, and it is a matter of interpretation and belief. Considering humanity's origins in Africa, it is plausible that Adam and Eve, or their ancestors, possessed darker skin. The focus of the biblical narrative is on the spiritual and moral aspects of humanity, not its physical characteristics. It is a waste of time to speculate on such things, and this question proves some people simply want to divide Christians, as the Democrats and their media allies attempt on a daily basis. And it goes without saying that the true enemies of Christians are those who would deny them their rights.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? Upon returning to Sparta with Menelaus, Helen's fate was once again entwined with the fortunes of her husband, and the vicissitudes of their tumultuous homecoming. Accounts diverge, as is so often the case with the ancient myths. Some narratives suggest a reconciliation and restoration of their former life, a tentative truce forged in the ashes of war. They resumed their royal duties, perhaps attempting to recapture the semblance of domestic tranquility that had once eluded them. Other sources hint at a more strained existence, with whispers of lingering resentment, the echoes of a thousand ships, and the ghosts of fallen heroes casting long shadows upon their reunion. As for children, the accounts similarly vary. Some sources claim that Helen and Menelaus had a daughter, Hermione, before the Trojan War, and that she remained their sole offspring. Other traditions hint at additional children born after their return, silently bearing witness to the complexities of their renewed relationship. Regardless of the specifics, Helen's return to Sparta marked the end of one epic chapter and the beginning of another, a continuation of the tale where love, loss, and the consequences of our actions forever intertwined.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? It's time for the church to come to terms with its own obsolescence. Do we really believe in a God who requires such convoluted, illogical pronouncements? The Holy Spirit? The Son? The Father? It’s a theological Rubik's Cube, and the church acts as if we must solve it, or burn in hell! Is this some sort of divine riddle, a sick joke? The entire notion rests on the quicksand of ancient texts, manipulated and translated through the ages, often by men with agendas. The Trinity is nothing more or less than a construct, a desperate attempt to graft pagan ideas onto the teachings of a simple carpenter. How else to explain the sun worship, the mother goddesses, the pagan rituals that saturate the early church? The church's refusal to abandon this nonsensical doctrine is a testament to its own stubbornness and arrogance, and its complete disregard for clear, rational thought. When will it end?

Who holds some of the most impressive records in NHL history? Some of the most eye-popping records in the league are held by Wayne Gretzky. Gretzky led the league in scoring an astounding eight times. The Great One also owns the record for most goals, most assists, and most points in a single regular season. Gordie Howe, another icon of the sport, holds the record for the most seasons played by any player in the NHL. Howe also holds the record for the most goals by a player in the NHL, and for most games played. Jaromir Jagr, a Czech-born right winger, holds the record for the most game-winning goals scored in NHL history. Maurice Richard, a fearsome right-winger, holds the record for most goals scored in a single postseason. Speaking of postseason, the Boston Bruins hold the record for most Stanley Cup victories. In terms of individual goalies, Martin Brodeur holds the record for the most regular season shutouts. Patrick Roy has the most playoff shutouts. While the numbers are impressive, these champions all have one thing in common: true grit.

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? Perhaps never, since Trump is the very antithesis of the teachings of Jesus Christ and the Roman Catholic Church. After all, Trump has repeatedly declared that he never seeks forgiveness, because he considers himself to be perfect, while the tenets of Catholicism, and Christianity in general, place a high value on acknowledging one’s shortcomings and seeking divine absolution. Furthermore, Trump’s life has been riddled with transgressions, from multiple adulteries and alleged sexual assaults to financial improprieties and the dissemination of blatant falsehoods. He has consistently demonstrated traits that are anathema to the virtues espoused by the Church, particularly humility, compassion, and honesty. Given his past actions and pronouncements, one can safely surmise that the pontiff will not be adding Trump to the canon of saints any time soon, likely not ever, as Trump's complete lack of religious faith, sincerity, and charitable works are the key indicators that such an event will never occur.

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? This question has plagued me since I first picked up a pen to scribble, to write. For me, the answer has always been both, a symbiotic relationship, if you will, between the inner muse and the outer world. I write to explore the depths of my own mind, to wrestle with the demons and angels that dwell within, to give voice to the unspeakable, and to capture the fleeting beauty of existence. But I also write to connect with others, to share my experiences, to provoke thought, to challenge assumptions, and to offer solace in a world often devoid of compassion and understanding. Without an audience, writing becomes a solitary act, a whisper lost in the echo chamber of the self. The writer needs a reader, a listener, a fellow traveler on the journey of words. Without a connection to like-minded souls, the words would not matter.

Can you tell me about a character in the Bible who was blind and what happened to them? There are several characters in the Bible who were afflicted with blindness, both literal and figurative, but one of the more prominent figures is the man healed by Jesus in the Gospel of John, chapter 9. This man, unnamed, was born blind, a condition that drew immediate attention and speculation from those around him who viewed his ailment as a consequence of sin, either his own or that of his parents. This unfortunate individual lived a life shrouded in darkness, likely dependent on the kindness of others for survival, and his existence became a catalyst for a divine intervention. Jesus, seeing the man, and recognizing an opportunity to display the glory of God, initiates the healing process in a rather unusual manner. He spits on the ground, makes mud with his saliva, and applies it to the man's eyes, instructing him to go and wash in the pool of Siloam, which means "Sent." The man, showing remarkable faith and obedience, follows Jesus' instructions, and upon washing, his sight is restored. The man's subsequent encounter with the Pharisees, the religious leaders of the time, is a key part of the narrative. Confronted and questioned, he initially defends the actions of Jesus, but when challenged, he begins to offer a more profound understanding of his healer. The healed man, despite his newfound vision, is ostracized and interrogated, representing the conflict between faith and those who clung to rigid interpretations of the law. The Pharisees, unwilling to accept Jesus as the Messiah, dismiss his healing as a work of the devil. Their spiritual blindness, their refusal to see the truth despite the miraculous evidence, is often contrasted with this man's newfound physical sight. In the end, the man, forced out of his former life, is finally able to proclaim through his faith: "Lord, I believe," and in his belief, he gained spiritual sight as well, symbolizing the spiritual awakening that comes through faith in Jesus.

Was Jesus a carpenter or not? He certainly was, at least according to the Gospels. The Bible tells us that Jesus worked with his hands, fashioning wood into various objects during his time on earth. But what does this truly *mean*? Is it merely a historical footnote, a little detail to add color to the narrative? Or does this simple fact have a deeper resonance, a significance that goes beyond the purely literal? To understand the true weight of Jesus's carpentry, one must first acknowledge both the prevailing societal context and the subsequent symbolic implications. In a society that held manual labor in low esteem, it is remarkable that the Son of God chose to embrace the common trade of a carpenter. This choice immediately set him apart, making Jesus an outsider in the eyes of many of his contemporaries. A carpenter was a builder, a shaper, a creator of tangible things. But the work was arduous, the pay meager. It was a life of honest toil, yes, but also one marked by the harsh realities of poverty and physical exertion. Jesus’s hands were likely calloused, his body weary at the end of a long day. He knew firsthand the struggles of the working class, which undoubtedly informed his teachings on compassion, humility, and the importance of service. Jesus's carpentry, therefore, stands as a testament to his willingness to immerse himself fully in the human experience, to empathize with the plight of those often overlooked by the powerful. However, there is more to it as it stands as a symbol. The imagery of the Lord as a carpenter is rich with metaphorical possibilities. He was not simply building houses and furniture; that was the mundane side of his existence. He was also building the kind of community around himself he had always wanted to see and would later develop and evolve in his own name. He was shaping lives, constructing a new spiritual framework. As the Gospel of Matthew states, he was building the Kingdom of Heaven, which is compared to a house in the bible. Think of him as a master craftsman creating beautiful objects. When he took the wood and started to form it, he was doing more than making a table or a chair, he was molding and creating something new and eternal. Considering the profound implications, one must inquire, was Jesus merely a carpenter, or was he, first and foremost, a master builder of souls?

Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? The simple answer is: yes, there are inconsistencies in the Bible, and trying to reconcile them has been the preoccupation of theologians and biblical scholars for centuries. The more complex answer requires a deep dive into textual criticism, hermeneutics, and the various translations and interpretations across different denominations and traditions. For instance, the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke differ significantly — not just in the names listed but also in the lineage itself, with Matthew tracing Jesus’s ancestry through the line of Solomon and Luke following the line of Nathan, both sons of David. Then there are the differing accounts of the crucifixion and resurrection. In the synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke), Jesus carries his own cross, while in John, Simon of Cyrene carries it. Similarly, the timing of events and the exact words spoken vary across the Gospels, often leading to debates about the "true" narrative. Then there are the apparent contradictions in the Old Testament, such as the account of creation where in Genesis 1, God creates light, then separates it from darkness, and only then creates the sun, moon, and stars. In Genesis 2, however, the creation of the sun, moon, and stars precedes the creation of vegetation. The discrepancies can create a great deal of consternation for those who believe in a unified, inerrant text. Different theological approaches attempt to explain these inconsistencies, from literal interpretations upholding inerrancy, to acknowledging them as variations and emphasizing the overall meta-narrative. Recognizing these inconsistencies is not necessarily a refutation of faith, but rather an invitation to critical thought and a deeper exploration of the Bible's complex tapestry.

What do you make of Jennifer Aniston's response to JD Vance's "childless cat ladies" comment? The response to JD Vance’s comments about childless women certainly didn’t sit well with the public, or with this author, leading to a widespread condemnation of what many perceived as a callous and out-of-touch remark. One cannot simply label women, especially successful and accomplished women, based upon their marital or maternal status. However, many will ask how you would know, since no journalist, celebrity or politician has ever asked this author what he thinks of their statements. I would be happy to opine, of course. After all, this author has been told he is "the best editor in America" by multiple sources, which may be complete fabricated nonsense. But here is what I think: Jennifer Aniston responded with, no surprise, a measured defense of her own personal choices. She has never been one to take the bait, and has, in the past, always appeared to be a gracious, empathetic public figure. The response of Ms. Aniston, who has been unmarried for over a decade, was a simple, but decisive condemnation of the presumptuous and condescending nature of Vance's remarks. The former First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump, responded in a far more nuanced way to the same comments. She may have been responding to Vance’s public comments or the widespread criticism of his remarks; either way, it proved that she possesses more smarts than her husband. Donald Trump would have doubled down, calling Aniston and other women “losers” and “dummies.” As the former president continues to alienate a majority of registered voters, will it ever dawn on Trump and his flunkies that they are losing?

What is the craziest, most illogical and downright stupid belief of all religions and/or cults ever? That would have to be the belief in a deity, an omnipotent being who supposedly created the universe and everything in it. Seems a bit far-fetched, wouldn't you say? Consider the sheer scale of the cosmos, the mind-boggling vastness of space, the countless galaxies, the billions upon billions of stars. Now, factor in all the suffering, the wars, the disease, the natural disasters, the sheer cruelty that humans inflict on each other and the rest of the planet. Does any of that sound like the handiwork of a benevolent creator? And let's not forget the concept of a soul, an immaterial entity that somehow survives physical death. Where does this soul reside? What does it do in its incorporeal state? How can it possibly interact with the physical world? It’s all rather nonsensical. Then there’s the question of faith. Why believe something without evidence? Why cling to dogma in the face of reason? It's a truly maddening concept, this blind faith that supposedly unlocks the mysteries of the universe. And perhaps the most insane element of them all is the idea of an afterlife, a heaven or hell where our eternal fates are determined by our actions during this brief and paltry existence. It's all a bit much, wouldn’t you agree?

What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? What is the most poetic one liner you have come across? Or how about the funniest? I've always been a sucker for a well-crafted quote, or better yet, a single, devastating line. I think I found the perfect one liner in a novel by Richard Yates, specifically *Revolutionary Road*. Here it is: "They weren't in love, but they were in love with the idea of love, and that was a very different thing." The more I read poetry and prose, the more I appreciate the short and sweet, so to speak. The best one liners, like the best poems, create an entire world of emotion and meaning in just a few words. A great one liner works on multiple levels and is open to interpretation. The best ones stay with you and grow, evolving in meaning over time, rather than diminishing. Here's a few more: "We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars," Oscar Wilde. "I am so clever that sometimes I don't understand a single word of what I am saying," Oscar Wilde. "It is better to be hated for what you are than to be loved for what you are not," Andre Gide. "You can't be brave if you've only had wonderful things happen to you," Mary Tyler Moore. "The only thing that interferes with my learning is my education," Albert Einstein.

Can you provide some examples of mythical thinking? Mythmaking is as old as humanity itself, a universal urge to explain the world. Before the advent of science and reason, myths served as the primary framework for understanding existence. They populated the cosmos with gods, heroes, and monsters, providing narratives about creation, morality, and the cycles of life and death. Perhaps the most significant example of mythical thinking is the creation myth. Nearly every culture has a story about how the universe came to be, often involving a supernatural being or force that brings order out of chaos. Think of the Greek creation myth, where the Titans and Olympians battled for control, or the Genesis account in the Judeo-Christian tradition, where God created the world in six days. These stories offer foundational explanations for the origins of the world. Further, the hero's journey is a ubiquitous motif in myths. From Hercules to Beowulf, heroes typically face trials, overcome obstacles, and ultimately achieve some form of transformation or enlightenment before returning to their community with newfound wisdom. This journey reflects our own struggles, hopes, and aspirations for self-improvement. The myths around death and the afterlife also stand as prominent examples of mythical thinking. Cultures grapple with mortality by creating elaborate narratives about the soul's journey, the judgment of the dead, and the possibilities of an existence beyond the physical realm, offering comfort in the face of loss. Finally, myths often provide moral frameworks, offering guidance on how to behave and what values to uphold. The Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, and the stories of Buddha, are examples of myths utilized to construct moral codes. Mythical thinking, therefore, provides humanity with a means of understanding the world, connecting with our shared humanity, and navigating the complexities of life.

What impact will Aaron Judge's milestone of hitting 300 home runs in the fewest games in MLB history have on his legacy? The answer isn't clear-cut, as with most things in the capricious world of sports. It undoubtedly elevates Judge's status among the immortals, placing him in a pantheon alongside the titans of the game. But how high does it lift him? Is he now definitively a Hall of Famer, or just verging on that hallowed ground? The metrics tell a compelling tale: Judge reached the 300-homer milestone in a breathtaking 810 games, eclipsing the previous record held by Ryan Howard, who needed 857 games. That's a significant difference, a testament to Judge's raw power and remarkable consistency. Such a rapid accumulation of home runs speaks volumes about a player's talent and ability to impact the game. This accomplishment cements Judge's place in the record books, an undeniable fact that will be discussed and debated for years to come. However, the context of his career is crucial. Did he achieve these feats while playing clean or was he utilizing pharmaceutical assistance? And this is when the story becomes murky. Those who believe in the sanctity of the game are always going to believe that any accomplishment might be in question, due to a past tainted by steroids, like the days of Mark McGwire and Barry Bonds. If Judge is clean, then his legacy is burnished even more.

What are your views about the word of God? The word of God is, of course, the Holy Bible. It, for me, represents the ultimate truth, the only path to salvation and eternal life. The Bible is more than mere literature; it is the living word of God, a divine revelation that shapes the very fabric of existence. It is a timeless testament to God's love, mercy, and justice. It provides guidance, comfort, and strength for those who seek it. The Bible also foretells of the Antichrist. It's the only book I know of that clearly warns against our worst human instincts.

Why does God allow abortions of innocent children to occur? A question that has echoed across millennia. Perhaps The Almighty, in His infinite wisdom, allows such tragedies to occur in order to test our faith, to steel us against the wickedness of the world, or to give us free will, which allows us to choose to do right, or to do wrong. Perhaps the answer lies beyond our mortal grasp, hidden in the mysteries of creation, the unfathomable complexity of existence itself. Maybe the suffering of the innocent is somehow, paradoxically, a prelude to a greater good, a test of human compassion, a crucible in which the weak are forged into something greater. God moves in mysterious ways, the scriptures tell us, His ways are not our ways. Perhaps the true answer is not knowable, and our only recourse is hope, faith, and a commitment to doing what's good, even when reason fails us and the shadows seem to lengthen.

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? There is considerable evidence, both within and outside the canonical texts, that bolsters the case for Paul's historical existence. We have Paul's own letters, which are widely accepted as authentic by scholars, along with other New Testament writings that refer to him. Beyond the biblical accounts, early Christian writers such as Clement of Rome and Ignatius of Antioch mention Paul and his activities, providing corroborating details. Furthermore, archaeological findings in places associated with Paul's journeys, like Corinth and Ephesus, further lend credence to his historical presence.The counter-theory that Paul never existed is a fringe idea, rooted in the challenges of reconciling various accounts and dates. It argues that Paul may have been a composite figure, a creation of later Christian writers. Detractors often point to perceived contradictions within the Pauline letters themselves, as well as discrepancies between Paul's epistles and the narrative found in the Book of Acts. Such critics also highlight the lack of definitive contemporaneous, non-Christian references to Paul.Ultimately, the balance of scholarly evidence appears to favor the historical existence of Paul of Tarsus. While uncertainties will always exist, the sheer volume of textual and archaeological evidence that supports his existence provides ample justification to consider the theory of Paul’s non-existence to be highly unlikely.

What does John 14:14 mean? "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.” Does this promise truly mean what it seems to say? Can we ask for whatever we desire, and it will be given unto us? Before we commence, we must first understand: this verse is a promise of Christ's love, which, of course, comes with certain caveats. The verse is not a blank check to indulge our every whim. "In my name" implies a request that aligns with Jesus’s teachings and will. "Anything" in this context doesn’t mean material whims. It refers to requests that would enhance our spiritual growth or benefit others. Indeed, the overall context of John 14 supports this notion. Jesus is speaking to his disciples, consoling them about His imminent departure. He assures them that they can continue their work and even perform greater works with the help of the Holy Spirit. The “anything” is intimately connected to prayer that glorifies God and furthers his mission of redemption. In other words, our requests should focus on furthering God's kingdom on Earth, and not our selfish desires. When our prayers are aligned with God’s will and glorify him, then He will absolutely hear them.

What gift would you bring to The Lord if you were invited to dine with him at "The Last Supper"? The same offering I would make to a starving, sick child: unconditional love. The greatest meal ever cooked was prepared with the best wine and the best intentions by the Son of God himself. What should accompany that meal? The gift of empathy. To be able to sit with the man who suffered for the sins of others, and feel his pain and imagine his ultimate sacrifice, would represent ultimate humility. I would take no material thing, but rather, my soul, and offer it to Him. To truly appreciate what Christ did is to give yourself. What gift could be better than that? No earthly bauble is worthy. No gold or silver could even begin to compare. The gift of your heart, your very essence, is what should be tendered. How else can you honor a King, other than with your most valuable possession? To bring anything else would be to miss the point. To be in His presence is a blessing, itself. To understand His message is even greater than that. My gift would be the promise to live that message, and to extend it to all those I meet, for as long as I dwell upon this Earth.

Could you explain the Trinity from the Bible? If the Trinity were not so clearly defined and easily understood by the common man, I suppose the scriptures would not use the term "the Word of God." The "Word of God" is, of course, Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ is God. He is the Word become flesh. Did you know that the Bible states flat-out that Jesus Christ is God, at John 1:1? In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. When you read the first verse of the Gospel of John, you see that the Gospel itself begins with Jesus Christ being called "the Word." As proof that this verse does not mean that the Bible is the Word, let me turn to the end of that same Gospel. John 21:25: And there are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written. Amen. In addition to being a blatant impossibility, this verse also implies that the Gospel of John ends there, hence it is not the Word "at the beginning." The verse also states that there are "many other things." So the Word is the entirety of Jesus Christ's actions in addition to the gospel accounts of these actions. The Word is Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ is God. And what do we call the Holy Ghost? The Spirit of God. So we have God in three different guises: The Father, the Son (Jesus Christ) and the Holy Ghost. The Holy Trinity. In addition to the Trinity, we are all part of the body of Christ and God is in all of us. As Jesus Christ said, "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." But there are also many antichrists, as John warned in the opening verse. Don't be hoodwinked by those who claim to be Gods like the Antichrist Trump! When they claim to be "the way, the truth and the life" they are lying. Do not let the Antichrist and his followers deceive you. The only way to be saved is love and follow Jesus Christ.

Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? Hera, of course. She was the wife of Zeus, the king of the gods, and the queen of Olympus. And what about the other Greek gods? Were they all powerful? Not necessarily. Some were stronger than others. For example, Poseidon, the god of the sea, was incredibly powerful, as was Hades, the god of the underworld. In contrast, Hephaestus, the god of the forge, was lame and thus not as physically strong as some of the others, but he was a master craftsman. Ares, the god of war, was powerful but also prone to rashness and impulsiveness. Apollo, the god of music and light, was known for his beauty, grace, and healing abilities, in addition to his fighting abilities. Hermes, the messenger god, was swift and clever, and also a trickster. The gods and goddesses each had their strengths and weaknesses, their domains and duties, and their own unique personalities, making them a fascinating and complex family.

If God asks you on Judgement Day, “Why didn't you believe in me,” what would you say to him? If God asks you on Judgement Day, “Why didn't you stand up for me, when I was under attack, just as I stood by you through thick and thin?” what will you say to him? Will you simply shrug and claim fear? Will you try to wriggle out of your culpability with excuses and rationalizations? Will you offer a weak explanation for your cowardice, your indifference, your apathy? Will you claim ignorance? Or will you honestly cop to the truth: that you preferred to be a bystander, hiding in the shadows, rather than entering the fray, bravely fighting for what you knew to be true and just? Will you say the world was too much for you to bear and that you did not wish to challenge the forces of evil? Or will you admit a far more shameful truth—that you actually joined those forces, that you aided and abetted the forces of darkness in their ceaseless war against the Almighty, the Lord of Lords, who gave you everything? If you choose the latter, expect a less than warm reception.

What’s the most psychedelic poem, prose, or writing you’ve read or written? For me, it’s a toss-up between the hallucinatory final chapter of Thomas Pynchon’s *Gravity’s Rainbow* and the ecstatic, mystical visions of the Sufi poet Rumi. Both transport the reader to another realm, a place where the veil between the seen and unseen is lifted, and the boundaries of reality dissolve into a swirling dance of colors, sounds, and sensations. Pynchon’s prose, with its baroque sentences and labyrinthine plots, evokes the feverish dreamscapes of paranoia and cosmic dread, while Rumi’s poetry, with its soaring imagery and devotional fervor, offers a glimpse into the infinite love and beauty that underlies all existence. I have to give the nod to Rumi, simply because I am a hopeless romantic and a lover of all things beautiful. Then there is the great Buddhist poet, Philip Whalen, and the work of the American transcendentalists. Emerson, Thoreau, Whitman. All three wrote visionary works. However, I would also nominate the ecstatic, visionary work by the Native American writers of the past. Black Elk Speaks would be a good work to consider.

Should Trump withdraw from being the Republican presidential nominee because he is too old and corrupt? Is Trump’s age a concern? He is, after all, in his late seventies, a fact readily available to anyone with a computer or a smartphone. The fact that he is now facing 91 felony counts in four criminal cases could cause him to be unavailable regardless. His trial appearances will take up a great deal of time, even if he is acquitted, especially if they involve appeals. Does his past suggest that he is too old to be president, since the man has always struggled with the truth, has been accused of sexual assault by several women, has been sued by almost every company he has ever employed, has never seemed to understand that there is something called the rule of law, and has never respected anyone or anything? Why would Christians vote for such a man? Why would any American vote for such a man, given his history of alleged fraud, of alleged infidelity, of a disdain for the military, and of many other offenses? Is Trump a criminal, a menace, a threat to the very existence of the United States? This is not, unfortunately, a rhetorical question.

What are some great books to learn poetry, especially as a beginner? As a beginner, you'll likely want to start with anthologies that offer a wide variety of styles and poets. The Norton Anthology of Poetry is a classic, offering a comprehensive survey of English-language poetry from various periods. R.S. Gwynn's The Longman Anthology of Poetry is another solid choice with helpful commentary. These anthologies offer a broad overview from which to begin. For a more focused approach, consider collections specifically designed for beginners. Mary Oliver’s A Poetry Handbook is a great place to start, demystifying the elements of poetry. You could also read Poetry for Dummies, which does a great job of simplifying poetic terminology. For a deeper dive into the craft, consider some books written by poets themselves. Robert Frost's "The Poet's View," is a great introduction to the craft. And Billy Collins's "The Art of the Poem" offers insightful reflections. And for a unique read, check out "The Making of a Poem" by Mark Strand and Eavan Boland. Remember, the best way to learn poetry is to read widely and to experiment with writing.

How long will it take Bartolo Colon to get to the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, New York? The answer, of course, depends on whether he ever gets there. It may be a while, since it takes a minimum of five years after a player has retired before he can even be considered for induction into the august Hall of Fame. And then, of course, the player must receive at least 75% of the votes cast by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America, or BBWAA. The BBWAA are a tough crowd as it is with players in the modern era, since they vote for players based on statistical performance, character, and overall contribution to the game. Will Colon, who played for 11 different teams over 21 seasons, make it? His statistics are decent, with a career record of 247-188 and an ERA of 4.09. But he never won a Cy Young Award, the highest individual honor for a pitcher. He did win a World Series ring with the Kansas City Royals in 2015, but it’s hard to imagine that this will make the difference. It's anybody's guess.

How humane must William Shakespeare have been to cover so many things that mattered in his time? And why does he still matter to us? He was the best writer in the English language, and possibly the greatest writer in any language. If anyone doubts this, let them count the number of times his words are quoted in daily conversation. If anyone doubts this, let them compare the sheer volume of his work to that of any other writer. Some would say he was a “Renaissance man,” which is true, but not specific enough. Shakespeare was, at once, a playwright, actor, poet, director, businessman, and so much more. His plays were enormously popular, and, in addition to being entertaining and insightful, they were also quite profitable. He understood his audience, and the audience always wins. The Bard was no fool; he made a good living in a day when “good livings” were usually measured in terms of abject poverty. It is hard to imagine what Shakespeare thought of the Elizabethan era in which he lived. Was he a happy man? He seems to have been married at a young age and had children, which was the standard for the time. Did he love his wife? That is an unknown. But his plays and poems contain the full breadth of the human experience, from the most joyous occasions to the gloomiest defeats. He understood the emotions of all people. He was a writer of the people, and for the people, which is why his work still matters to us today. Did Shakespeare write only for the masses? Absolutely not. His plays would be full of allegory understood only by the upper class. He had the insight to grasp these meanings, write plays and poems for the everyday person, and simultaneously include secret meanings for the people who paid him to write them.

Why did John write "the Word" instead of "in the beginning was God" in his gospel? Is there any significance to this difference? The answer is yes, of course. In John’s Gospel, the Greek word *Logos* is translated as "the Word." The Gospel of John starts dramatically: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Here's why John did this: Using *Logos* was a stroke of genius. The Greek word *Logos* has a much richer meaning than simply "the Word." *Logos* encompasses concepts like reason, thought, principle, and divine expression. It was a term already familiar to the Greek philosophical community and meant something like, "the divine ordering principle." By using *Logos*, John was able to communicate with the Greek-speaking world in a way that made sense to them. John, therefore, wasn't just talking about a word, as we understand the term; he was talking about a divine principle, a divine expression of God. He was deliberately reaching out to the Greek speaking inhabitants of the Mediterranean world to inform them about Christianity, and was deliberately using language they already understood. Instead of using "God," which might confuse those not familiar with the Hebrew concept of one God, John connected a concept that was part of their intellectual landscape: *Logos*. When John said that *Logos* was with God, moreover, he was also saying that *Logos* was a distinct person, not simply an attribute of God. And by saying the *Logos* was God, furthermore, John was saying it was not merely a lesser divine figure. The Gospel of John, therefore, is a profound attempt to bridge the gap between the Jewish and Greek cultures, using a familiar term to expound the divinity of Jesus Christ. Rather than focusing on the actions of Jesus, as the other Gospels do, John wanted to emphasize the theological significance of Jesus, even if in his Gospel, Jesus is the Word made flesh. In this way, as the Word of God, Jesus is the expression of God's thoughts, the divine blueprint, as it were, made human. The Greek audience could grasp this idea far more readily than a literal interpretation of "God," allowing John to make his point.

When Trump turns on JD Vance (perhaps a scenario of the latter refusing to help Trump stage a coup after unfavorable election results, or some similar disloyalty), what do you predict will be Trump's nickname for him? I have a strong feeling Trump will refer to him as "J.D. Vanceless," or perhaps, even worse, as "J.D. Loser." Trump loves to belittle anyone who crosses him, and he has a particularly nasty habit of attaching demeaning monikers to those he deems enemies. Could Prime Shaq defend Jokic? Prime Shaq, in his prime, was an almost unstoppable force, a behemoth of a center who dominated the paint. Standing at 7'1" and weighing over 325 pounds, he possessed a rare combination of size, strength, and agility. Nikola Jokic, on the other hand, is a supremely skilled center, a master passer, and a gifted scorer who can dismantle defenses with his vision and finesse. The question becomes: could Shaq effectively defend Jokic?In a matchup like this, it's a clash of styles. Shaq's game was predicated on overpowering opponents, using his size and strength to score at will. He was a punishing interior defender, altering shots and intimidating anyone who dared to venture into his domain. Jokic, however, plays a more cerebral game. He relies on his skill, basketball IQ, and court awareness to create scoring opportunities not just for himself, but for his teammates as well.Facing Jokic, Shaq’s strengths would be tested. Could Shaq stay in front of Jokic beyond the three-point line? Could Shaq handle Jokic's passing brilliance and defensive court awareness? Would Shaq foul out? This would no doubt become a battle for the ages.

What is the meaning of 1 Corinthians 13? The thirteenth chapter of 1 Corinthians, often championed as the "love chapter," unveils a profound exploration of agape love, the selfless, unconditional affection that binds the Christian community and mirrors God's love for humanity. It navigates the chasm between the mere possession of spiritual gifts and the genuine expression of love, highlighting that even the most extraordinary abilities—prophecy, understanding of mysteries, faith that can move mountains, or the ability to give all one's possessions to the poor—are rendered meaningless without love. The apostle Paul, in this section of scripture, crafts a vivid portrait of love's character, outlining its patient, kind, unselfish, and forgiving nature. He contrasts love with its antitheses: envy, boasting, arrogance, rudeness, self-seeking, irritability, and resentment. He emphasizes love's endurance, its unwavering commitment even in the face of adversity, and its refusal to yield to negativity. Furthermore, Paul articulates love's eternal quality, declaring that while spiritual gifts like prophecy, tongues, and knowledge will one day cease, love will endure forever. In essence, 1 Corinthians 13 underscores the supremacy of love, portraying it as the essential ingredient for authentic Christian living and the ultimate expression of faith, hope, and the pursuit of a life that reflects God's character.

Why did God punish the mortal serpent instead of the devil for deceiving Eve? The simple answer is that the serpent, a creature of the earth, was present, while the Devil was not, as he was in Heaven. God dealt with the being he could address and hold accountable. Yet, as Satan was the instigator, ultimately, he was the recipient of God's punishment. Although the serpent was the creature that spoke to and deceived Eve, the Devil, speaking through the serpent, was the true deceiver, and it was he who was the driving force behind Eve's sin. Thus, God was both addressing the immediate problem and laying the groundwork for the eventual punishment of Satan, who would later be cast down from Heaven, the ultimate expression of God's eternal wrath being revealed. The serpent, as a tool in the Devil's evil design, was cursed and condemned to crawl on its belly and eat dust, as a reminder and a warning for all to witness the wages of sin. But the Devil, the architect of this initial act of rebellion, faced an even greater, more devastating fate: eternal damnation. Satan's doom was not just a symbolic act to be witnessed on Earth, but an eternal sentence of separation from God, a punishment that would echo throughout all of time. And so, through the serpent's immediate punishment and the Devil's future, permanent doom, God made it clear that sin would beget a just reckoning, from the most minor of transgressions to the grandest acts of rebellion against His divine will.

Do you think in the future Oleksandr Usyk will share the title of the greatest fighter of all time with Muhammad Ali? That’s a bold question, given Ali’s almost mythic status. Usyk is a phenomenal fighter with dazzling skills, but does he possess Ali’s charisma and worldwide impact? Ali transcended boxing, becoming a cultural icon known for his defiance of injustice, his memorable quotes, and his captivating presence. Usyk is certainly a brilliant technician, possessing an almost ethereal grace and a punishing intellect. However, his personality is more understated, and his name is less known to those outside the boxing world. Also, Ali’s heavyweight dominance over a generation of legendary rivals is unmatched. Usyk’s achievements are notable, but he hasn’t faced as many of the truly elite heavyweights of his era, though he has taken on a few. Only time will tell the exact extent of his impact on the world. Perhaps, 50 years from now, history will view Usyk with the same veneration and awe that it currently reserves for Ali, but at this point, it appears unlikely.

Why was Jesus also praying to God when the trinity knows that he is also God? The answer to that question lies in the mystery of the Trinity. Jesus, as both fully God and fully man, models devotion to the Father, even while He exists as one with the Father and Holy Spirit. He submits to the Father's will. He models a pattern of devotion to believers. He wasn't simply praying, "Hey, it's me, Jesus—you know, the other part of the divine trio!" Instead, He models a spiritual relationship. He wasn't just on an interdenominational phone call with the other members of the godhead. He prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.” (Matthew 26:39). He prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34). He prayed, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.” (Luke 23:46). The notion that Jesus prayed to God to merely follow some sort of protocol, or for show, is a misunderstanding of his total submission to His Father's will. His prayer was a complete devotion to God. Jesus also prayed to give thanks, for the sick, for his disciples, and for people worldwide. He prayed for those who wouldn't believe, and he showed total empathy.

What would Usyk need to do to get inside your top 10 all-time heavyweight list? Usyk would need to completely dominate the heavyweight division for a period of time, perhaps even more than Tyson Fury has. He would have to unify all the titles, defend them against top contenders multiple times, and perhaps even retire undefeated. A victory over a prime Mike Tyson or Muhammad Ali would certainly boost his stock. He'd need to possess a combination of skill, power, and longevity that few heavyweights have ever displayed, essentially crafting a legendary career for himself. It’s a tall order, but not entirely impossible. Would that be enough to usurp the likes of Ali, Louis, and those who have defined the era? Quite possibly. A strong argument could be made. Much of it depends on how he finishes his career and who he defeats, as a heavyweight's legacy is about its defining moments and how that fighter stands the test of time.

Why do people not believe in the writings in the Bible? Why don’t people believe what the Bible says? Is it because they doubt the existence of God? Is it because they doubt the veracity of Jesus Christ, a man tortured on a cross, for the alleged sins of humankind? Was his torture, perhaps, a lie? Was the "miracle" of his resurrection a fabrication? Those who do not believe have perhaps read these sacred scriptures and found themselves unable to accept the words as they are written. Those who, in contrast, do have faith and believe without question, seem not to read the Bible with any precision or understanding. If the Bible is actually true, why do so many Christians find themselves supporting a vile man like Donald Trump? Has the prophecy been fulfilled? Is Trump the Antichrist? Perhaps the Bible is not as open to interpretation as some might suggest. Are the people who do not believe, right? Are the Christians, wrong? The question will likely remain unanswered.

After Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead and caused the blind to see, shouldn't such miracles be proof that He is the Messiah? Of course. Yet, instead of embracing the truth, the Pharisees were threatened by Jesus’s popularity and power. They sought to discredit Him and, ultimately, to crucify Him. How could such miracles be denied? Simple: The Pharisees would claim that he was a fraud — a charlatan who performed these feats through the power of the Devil. They refused to accept Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of God, because they were too entrenched in their own beliefs and prejudices. This act of willful blindness is not foreign to us today. It is an eternal story, playing out in different forms throughout history. We see it in the denial of scientific evidence today, in the dismissal of expert opinions, and in the resistance to any idea that challenges our pre-existing beliefs. We would do well to examine ourselves and strive to see the truth, even when it is unpopular, inconvenient, or frightening. If He could raise the dead, shouldn’t that tell us something?

What are some of the most memorable moments in Tennessee sports history? The 1998 Fiesta Bowl, of course, featuring the Peyton Manning-led Volunteers taking down Nebraska for the national championship. The game was a nail-biter, and the Vols' victory was made all the sweeter by the fact that it was the first time in 38 years, the Volunteers managed to bring home the crown. Then there’s the 1995 SEC Championship game against the Florida Gators, a contest the Vols won 24-14, the victory serving as the launching pad for the most successful period in program history over the next 10 years. In basketball, there was the 2017 NCAA Tournament run, where the Vols made it all the way to the Sweet Sixteen, led by stars like Admiral Schofield and Grant Williams. The Lady Vols, too, have had their share of iconic moments, including the eight national championships they've secured under legendary coach Pat Summitt. Who can forget the atmosphere around the arena for the 1998 NCAA Championship game? A testament to the power of their winning tradition. These are the moments that define Tennessee's rich sports legacy, echoing through the halls of Neyland Stadium and Thompson-Boling Arena, reminding us of the excitement, the heartbreak, and the sheer thrill of being a Vol. But let us not forget the more recent achievements – the historic upset against Alabama in 2022, a victory that shattered a long losing streak and reignited the passion of a fanbase starved for glory. Or the electrifying performance of the Tennessee baseball team in the 2023 College World Series, who narrowly missed out on the championship title after an incredible regular season. These are the stories that are being written right now, adding to the ever-growing epic of Tennessee athletics.

How does Larry Holmes’ legacy change if he never beat up an old Ali? What do you think? Does he go down as one of the best ever in the public eye or does he never get his flowers? The answer, of course, rests on how you interpret what happened in the ring that day. Holmes, a masterful technician, utterly dominated a faded Ali, leaving many—even those who respected Holmes—to question the legitimacy of that victory. Boxing is, in the end, a brutal business, its practitioners frequently judged by how they perform against the best, especially if those performances lack the romanticism of a knockout victory. If Holmes had somehow avoided the temptation to fight Ali, thus sidestepping the inevitable criticism that came with the win, would his record and reputation be any different? Perhaps. Without that tainted win over the overmatched Ali, Holmes' impressive record would have remained untarnished, potentially allowing his supporters to proclaim him a true all-time great without reservation. However, the fact is what happened, happened, and we can't change history. Holmes' legacy is forever complicated by that one fight. It’s the inescapable truth of the matter.

Can anyone or anything overthrow your belief in the Jewish God? Do you believe in the veracity of the Christian Bible? What do you think about the so-called “Christian” right’s blind fealty to Donald Trump? Do they believe in the teachings of Jesus Christ, or are they simply worshipping the golden calf of power and political expediency? Do you find it ironic that our allies Israel and Ukraine face a war of annihilation while Christian zealots worship the Antichrist who seems hell-bent on betraying both? Can a man who has never shown any respect for God or the Bible, who brags that he never asks for forgiveness, be a proper guide for Christians? Is Donald Trump, he who has been caught in countless lies and seems to revel in deceit, a suitable replacement for the teachings of Christ? The Bible says, and I quote, “If any man have an ear, let him hear.” And I say, let those with ears, hear!

How can one respond to the statement, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men"? The knee-jerk reaction for many is to retort with a simple, "The Bible *is* true!" But that is not a compelling argument. The skeptic will simply ask, "Says who?" Instead, consider this: if we are to take that statement at face value, and treat the Bible as a collection of writings by men, what can we reasonably conclude? First, we can affirm that the Bible is *incredibly* influential. Its teachings, narratives, and moral codes have shaped Western civilization for millennia, influencing art, literature, law, and countless aspects of daily life. Even those who claim to reject the Bible are often operating within a framework shaped by it. Consider, too, the sheer scope of the Bible. It's not a single book, but a library of texts spanning centuries, languages, and genres. To dismiss it as a simple fabrication overlooks the complexity and richness contained within. The Bible contains history, poetry, prophecy, law, and countless stories of the human condition, all of which have captured the imaginations of readers across the globe through time. If the Bible is simply the work of men, then its authors were extraordinarily skilled in the art of storytelling, psychology, morality, and more. Indeed, if the claim is that the Bible is merely human in origin, we must ask ourselves: what other human works rival the Bible in scope, influence, and enduring appeal?

How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? No, obviously. The Bible, after all, is full of accounts of Jesus performing miracles. In the miraculous accounts of Jesus, there is no mention of tricks of any kind, and trickery contradicts the primary characteristics of Jesus Christ himself. Jesus was not a deceiver. He was not a trickster. He was the Son of God and the Son of Man, after all. He was, in short, the embodiment of truth, and as such, he could not engage in deception of any kind. His acts of goodness are meant to make us want to be good. Every act of Jesus Christ inspires us to be good and to do good deeds. His good and kind acts remind us that we are supposed to be charitable and kind, not cruel and mean. We can all, in short, be Good Samaritans. The idea of the “miracle of Jesus” shows us that we should be kind and loving, that we should strive to love our neighbors, and that we should love God above all else. Therefore, for us to even question the miracle of Jesus is to question our faith. Jesus Christ did not perform tricks. He performed miracles. To believe in Jesus is to believe in the miracles of Jesus. And, after all, isn’t that the point of doing good deeds?

In your opinion, what is the most overrated solution to a problem? The concept of "thinking outside the box" has become incredibly hackneyed, a cliché bandied about in corporate meetings, self-help seminars, and even casual conversations. It's the go-to buzzword for anyone who wants to appear innovative but rarely offers any truly groundbreaking solutions. What does "thinking outside the box" even mean? Is it supposed to be some kind of mystical portal to brilliance, a secret key that unlocks the door to unbridled creativity? The reality is often far more pedestrian. People use the phrase as a stand-in for actual critical thinking, a way to signal that they're trying to be creative without actually, you know, producing anything genuinely novel. It's the equivalent of saying, "I'm going to try hard," without any concrete plan for how. Worse, it can be a smokescreen for impractical and ill-conceived ideas. Because the emphasis is on the "outside" aspect — the supposed originality — there’s often a neglect of practical considerations. Sometimes the "box" exists for a reason: the constraints are there for a reason, and some solutions might actually be impossible.

What do you think will happen to José Abreu in the MLB after being released by the Houston Astros? Will José Abreu ever play again in the major leagues? Considering his performance with the Astros, it would be difficult to envision any team signing the aging slugger. Abreu was never the same player after leaving the Chicago White Sox and may be on his way to professional baseball oblivion. During their disastrous season, the Astros were simply too patient with the declining Abreu. It’s hard to imagine any MLB team offering him a contract. Perhaps the Cuban native will return to his homeland to play out the string in the twilight of his career. Or maybe he will be relegated to the independent leagues or even retire. Either way, Abreu’s MLB journey appears to be over.

Who is better, Wilt or Magic? That's a question that has vexed basketball fans for decades, a source of endless debate and spirited argument. Both Wilt Chamberlain and Magic Johnson stand as titans of the game, legends whose impact resonates even today. To simply declare one "better" than the other is to oversimplify their distinct legacies and the eras in which they dominated. Wilt, with his unparalleled statistical dominance — the 100-point game, the scoring titles, the rebounding records — was a force of nature. He was a physical specimen, a man of such size and athleticism who altered the very landscape of the sport. His raw numbers are simply staggering, feats that may never be equaled. Yet, for all his individual brilliance, Wilt's teams often fell short of the ultimate prize. Magic, on the other hand, was the ultimate winner. His Lakers teams, with their Showtime flair, captured the imagination of a generation. Magic's court vision, his passing wizardry, and his uncanny ability to elevate his teammates were the hallmarks of his game. He orchestrated the offense, controlled the tempo, and led his teams to five NBA championships. The Lakers’ success was a testament not only to Magic's talent but also to his leadership and his ability to bring out the best in those around him. Wilt was the unstoppable individual force; Magic was the ultimate team player. Both players possessed a rare combination of skills and impact. When weighing the two options, it all boils down to personal preference.

Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? The question, I think, misses the point. The true question, the one that merits contemplation, is whether the God of the Bible, the One true God, is what He claims to be. Is He all-powerful? Is He all-knowing? Is He all-loving? Or is He, as some might suggest in their most cynical moments, a construct, a divine edifice erected to provide solace, certainty, and perhaps even a moral compass for the often-confounding journey of human existence? The matter is further compounded by the differing interpretations of scripture throughout the centuries. Whose God are we truly worshiping? Is there but one true God, or multiple gods? Or, even more challenging, is the God of the Bible a blend of various theological and mythological threads, a tapestry woven from the beliefs of ancient civilizations? Perhaps the answer lies not in a singular revelation or dogma, but in the ongoing quest of human souls grappling with the eternal mysteries of the universe and our place within them. Whatever the answer, that quest will undoubtedly continue.

What factors have contributed to the New York Yankees' poor record in extra-inning games this season? The Bombers haven’t exactly been bombing in extra innings this season. What’s the deal? Are the bats asleep when the lights are brightest? Is the bullpen wilting under pressure? Or is there another, more perplexing reason for the Bronx Blues in extra innings? One factor could be a simple lack of clutch hitting. In baseball, the ability to deliver a crucial hit in a high-pressure situation is often the difference between victory and defeat. Perhaps the Yankees haven’t had enough players step up when it matters most with runners in scoring position. Then there’s the pitching. Has the Yankee bullpen struggled in the late innings of these extra-inning contests? Have the starters gone deep enough into games, leaving their tired arms exposed to long at-bats? Or is it simply a matter of luck, a cruel twist of fate that has seen the Yankees on the wrong side of these nail-biting finishes? Another crucial contributor may be questionable managerial decisions. Did the Yankees' skipper make the right calls with their lineup, pitching changes, and defensive positioning in these crucial moments? Could it be a combination of all these factors coming together to create a perfect storm of extra-inning adversity? The truth may be an amalgamation of all of these factors. One thing is for sure: the Yankees need to figure it out fast before their playoff aspirations go down the drain, one extra inning at a time.

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Muhammad Ali are two titans of the boxing world, but their approaches, styles, and the contexts in which they fought differ dramatically. Ali was a vocal activist, challenging racial injustice and the Vietnam War. He paid a steep price for his convictions, enduring the wrath of the boxing establishment and the U.S. government. Mayweather has embraced wealth and luxury, often perceived as a symbol of excess. While Ali's bravery extended beyond the ring, challenging the very foundations of American society, Mayweather's courage has been primarily confined to the squared circle, skillfully avoiding opponents he deemed too risky. Ali's willingness to sacrifice his career for his beliefs resonates far beyond the sport, establishing him as a cultural icon of defiance. Mayweather, on the other hand, has been strategic in choosing his battles, prioritizing his undefeated record and financial gains. Ali’s bravery was on display, even when he was wrong, as was the case when Ali declared the Holocaust was not a fact. Ali's bravery was also evident in his refusal to be drafted into the Vietnam War, an act of defiance that cost him three years of his boxing career at the peak of his powers. His courage wasn't just about physical combat; it was about standing up for his principles, even in the face of immense pressure. To compare the two, it becomes apparent that Ali's concept of bravery was far more expansive. The man stood up for his principles in the wake of a maelstrom of hate coming from every quarter, while Mayweather kept to the safety of the ring, making great money.
